The core insight is that behavioral inconsistency does not arise solely from deficit in instinctual drive but also from excessive instinctual load. This is formalized through a stochastic kernel where inhibition strength I modulates behavioral variance B. The social isolation instinct S_ij introduces gendered asymmetry into interpersonal dynamics, forming a gender-specific modulation factor G. Habituation H acts as a memory-dependent inhibitor, reducing the likelihood of instinctual reassertion beyond a threshold T. These primitives form a triadic system where each component interacts dynamically—instincts generate variance, habits suppress it, and gendered social norms modulate both. The resulting model captures dualities in behavioral regulation: over-inhibition leads to rigidity, under-inhibition to impulsivity. Failure modes emerge when habituation becomes pathological (e.g., habitual desensitization), or when gendered norms fail to align with evolving social structures. The mathematical structure supports both Bayesian inference for GSI and state-transition logic for GSE.
